newsitem.title: USA: Clinton signs birth bill; Dole ad hits "liberal".
newsitem.headline: Clinton signs birth bill; Dole ad hits "liberal".

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

President Bill Clinton signed a popular bill on Thursday guaranteeing women 48 hours' hospital stay after childbirth and Republican Bob Dole began airing a commercial calling Clinton a "tax-and-spend liberal."

Dole's television advertisement listed some Clinton spending measures including $76 million on "midnight basketball" for inner city youths and said: "The real Bill Clinton? A real tax-and-spend liberal."
Dole trails Clinton by 12 to 15 percentage points in national polls and is behind in almost all key battleground states.
Clinton relished the opportunity presented by yet another Rose Garden bill-signing ceremony.

"Parents may rush to the hospital, but they shouldn't be rushed out of it unless it's the right thing to do for the parent and the child. This law is common sense, and now it is the law of the land," he said in signing the "Newborns' and Mothers' Protection Act" that requires health insurers to let women stay in the hospital for 48 hours after a normal delivery and 96 hours after a Caesarean.
The measure was tied to a $64.4 billion government money bill that also improves health benefits for mental patients and children with spina bifida born to Vietnam veterans.
Clinton's soaring political fortunes got a further boost with the release of annual census data on household income.

"In one year, median household income was up $898 after inflation. That's the biggest increase in a decade. Over the last two years, the typical American family has seen its income rise $1,600 over inflation," Clinton said.

A survey of state polls conducted by the Hotline political newsletter found Clinton leading in 36 states with 416 votes in the Electoral College, where 270 are needed to win the presidency. Dole led in 13 states with 87 electoral votes.

Dole kicked off a trip to the must-win state of Florida at a home for senior citizens, accusing Clinton of a "Mediscare" campaign to frighten the elderly over Medicare. He blasted Democratic television ads blanketing the state as a campaign to frighten senior citizens by claiming Republicans would slash Medicare health care for the elderly.

"We're trying to save, preserve and strengthen Medicare and not destroy it," he said after dropping in on lunch at the Fountainview Senior Citizens Community. "So I would challenge the president: Stop running all those scare ads. Stop trying to scare people."

Dole's current schedule in Florida is leisurely, with no major campaign events on his calendar for the next few days as he prepares for his first televised debate with Clinton, to be held in Hartford, Connecticut, a week from Sunday.

The Clinton and Dole campaigns continued to wrangle over the presidential debates, with Dole's campaign manager, Scott Reed, accusing Clinton of wanting to have the fewest possible debates in front of the smallest possible audience.

The Dole campaign wants to move up the time of the second debate, scheduled for Oct. 16 in San Diego, by 45 minutes to avoid clashing with a baseball playoff game. It also wants the candidates to stand behind a "writing platform" to accomodate Dole, who has difficulty taking notes because of a war wound.
